lesson.title: Turning a Sample Into a Single Number: The Test Statistic
lesson.summary: A test statistic standardizes how far a sample result sits from what the null hypothesis predicts, measured in standard errors, so that results from any scale can be judged on one common z scale.
lesson.body:
You already know that a z-score measures how many standard deviations a value sits from a mean. A test statistic applies that same idea to hypothesis testing: it measures how many standard errors your sample statistic, such as a sample mean x-bar or sample proportion p-hat, sits from the value the null hypothesis claims. The general recipe for a z test statistic is

z = (sample statistic minus null value) divided by (standard error of the sample statistic)

The numerator captures how far your data landed from what H0 predicted. Dividing by the standard error rescales that gap into units of ordinary sampling variability. A gap of two ounces means very little if boxes routinely vary by five ounces, and it means a great deal if they routinely vary by one tenth of an ounce, the test statistic is what lets you tell the difference.

Return to the cereal box example: the company claims a mean of mu = 16 ounces, the machine's known standard deviation is sigma = 0.3 ounces, and a sample of n = 36 boxes produced a sample mean of x-bar = 15.9 ounces. For a mean, the formula is z = (x-bar minus mu) divided by (sigma divided by the square root of n). The standard error is 0.3 divided by the square root of 36, which is 0.3 divided by 6, or 0.05. The test statistic is then (15.9 minus 16) divided by 0.05, which is negative 0.1 divided by 0.05, or z = negative 2.00. In words, the sample mean fell exactly two standard errors below the claimed value. Under a normal model, gaps that large happen a small fraction of the time by chance alone, which is exactly why this result raises suspicion that the machine is not centered where the company claims.

The same logic applies to proportions with a different standard error formula: z = (p-hat minus p0) divided by the square root of (p0 times (1 minus p0), all divided by n). Suppose you wanted to check whether a coin is fair, H0: p = 0.5, and you flip it 100 times, getting 62 heads, so p-hat = 0.62. The standard error is the square root of (0.5 times 0.5 divided by 100), which is the square root of 0.0025, or 0.05. The test statistic is (0.62 minus 0.5) divided by 0.05, which is 0.12 divided by 0.05, or z = 2.40. Same structure, different variability rule, because proportions and means do not spread out the same way.

A test statistic on its own does not yet answer the question "is this significant." It is an input to the p-value, which turns that standardized distance into an actual probability, the subject of the next chapter. Recall also that the whole logic of a hypothesis test is to assume H0 is true and ask how surprising the observed data would be under that assumption. The test statistic is the tool that puts a precise, comparable number on "how surprising."
